Russian media say the large ticks have become particularly active across regions including Rostov, Krasnodar, Stavropol, Astrakhan and Kalmykia.

Some reports also claim the ticks are far less responsive to standard repellents than ordinary species.

text:
Interesting: Friedemann Weber’s CCHFV VLP System 

Friedemann Weber was part of a 2015 research team that developed a transcriptionally competent virus-like particle system for Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus. The team included Stephanie Devignot, Éric Bergeron, Stuart T. Nichol, Ali Mirazimi, and Friedemann Weber.

The system used key CCHFV components — L polymerase, N nucleocapsid protein, Gn/Gc glycoproteins, and a reporter minigenome — to generate virus-like particles that could model parts of the viral life cycle without requiring full infectious wild-type virus in every experiment.

The main purpose was functional virology, not direct vaccine production. The system helped researchers study viral entry, transcription, replication, assembly, and release. A central finding was that the endonuclease domain of the CCHFV L protein, especially around residue D693, was important for viral transcription and cap-snatching.

In short:

▪️ CCHFV tc-VLP system = research platform
Purpose = study virus function under controlled conditions

▪️ Key finding = L-protein endonuclease required for transcription

▪️ Relevance = reverse genetics, antiviral research, vaccine-adjacent immunology

▪️ Not the same as = a licensed vaccine or proof of historical origin claims

A concise caption:

In 2015, Stephanie Devignot, Éric Bergeron, Stuart Nichol, Ali Mirazimi, and Friedemann Weber developed a transcriptionally competent CCHFV virus-like particle system.

It allowed researchers to study key steps of the CCHFV life cycle and identified the L-protein endonuclease region, including residue D693, as crucial for transcription. 

The system was mainly a reverse-genetics research tool, later relevant to vaccine and immunology research, but not itself a licensed vaccine.

text:
Over 100 people have been hospitalised in Meru after consuming contaminated meat.

What this reveals is a deeper vulnerability in how food moves from farm to table.

What’s Happening

1. Mass Exposure  
117 people were hospitalised in Meru County after eating meat from a cow that died of anthrax.

2. Confirmed Cases  
At least 8 individuals have tested positive, with more results pending.

3. Point of Failure  
The animal had died before slaughter—yet still entered the food chain.

4. Health Response  
Medical teams are managing patients while investigations and containment measures continue.

Why This Matters

1. Informal Supply Chains  
Unregulated slaughter and meat distribution remain a major public health risk.

2. Cost vs Safety Tradeoff  
“Salvaging” meat from dead animals is often driven by economic pressure—but carries serious consequences.

3. Zoonotic Threats  
Diseases like anthrax don’t just affect livestock—they cross into human populations quickly.

4. Surveillance Gaps  
Detection often happens after exposure, not before.

What To Watch

1. Sudden Livestock Deaths  
Never consume or handle animals that die unexpectedly.

2. Meat Sources  
Avoid unverified vendors, especially during outbreak alerts.

3. Symptoms  
Skin lesions, severe stomach issues, or breathing complications require immediate medical attention.

4. Local Advisories  
Follow county health updates on quarantines and safe zones.

The Bigger Picture

Africa’s food systems are evolving:

• Informal markets → regulated supply chains  
• Reactive healthcare → preventive surveillance  
• Livestock economy → public health interface  

Food safety is no longer just an agricultural issue.

It’s a national health priority.

Bottom Line

This isn’t just a local outbreak.

It’s a system warning.

What enters the food chain determines what enters the healthcare system.

text:
🌍 WHO reports anthrax outbreaks in 5 East and Southern African countries, resulting in 20 deaths

Five countries in East and Southern Africa are in the middle of outbreaks of the anthrax disease, with more than 1,100 suspected cases and 20 deaths this year, the World Health Organization said.

A total of 1,166 suspected cases had been reported in Kenya, Malawi, Uganda, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Thirty-seven cases had been confirmed by laboratory tests.

WHO said the five countries have seasonal outbreaks every year, but Zambia was experiencing its worst since 2011 and Malawi reported its first human case this year. Uganda had reported 13 deaths.

Anthrax usually affects livestock like cattle, sheep and goats, as well as wild herbivores. Humans can be infected if they are exposed to animals or contaminated animal products. Anthrax isn't generally considered to be contagious between humans, although there have been rare cases of person-to-person transmission.

text:
In North Eastern Kenya, human beings are queuing for muddy water like livestock.

Wajir.
Marsabit.
Garissa.
Mandera.
Isiolo.

Mothers are digging dry riverbeds with bare hands. Children are drinking brown water crawling with disease. Families are sleeping hungry while trucks carrying relief supplies are turned into political theatre.

And yet when “high table dignitaries” land in choppers, suddenly there is clean bottled water. Suddenly there is food. Suddenly tents, chairs, security, and protocol appear from nowhere.

The same residents who have not had clean water for months are expected to serve tea.
The same communities surviving on relief maize are expected to clap.
The same people walking 10 kilometers for water are expected to kneel before politicians who arrive for photo sessions.

It is humiliation layered on suffering.

This is not drought alone.
This is neglect.
This is engineered abandonment.

North Eastern Kenya has been treated like a voting bloc during elections and a forgotten desert after results are announced. Billions are allocated on paper. Projects are launched. Speeches are made. But on the ground? Dry taps. Empty boreholes. Starving families.

When residents protest over water and food shortages, they are labeled restless. When they demand accountability, they are called ungrateful. When they refuse to clap, they are seen as disrespectful.

But let’s be honest:

A hungry population owes no applause.
A thirsty community owes no hospitality.
A neglected region owes no loyalty to leaders who remember them only during campaigns.

It is morally bankrupt for the political class to sit at “high tables” while the people who elected them are scraping mud for survival.

Water is not a privilege.
Food is not a favor.
Dignity is not negotiable.

If this country can fund luxury convoys, endless allowances, and bloated government offices, it can drill boreholes. It can build dams. It can ensure food security. The problem is not resources. The problem is priorities.

North Eastern Kenya does not need pity.
It needs infrastructure.
It needs accountability.
It needs leadership that shows up before cameras do.

Until then, every glass of bottled water served to a visiting dignitary in those counties should taste like shame.

Today in Turkana County, we delivered over 100 modern beehives to farmer groups from Loima and Turkana Central to support commercial honey production.

I highlighted the Government’s strategic drought response, including the release of KSh 500 million for animal feeds and the submission of a KSh 5.8 billion budget for water tracking, veterinary medicines, vaccines and other animal health interventions.

I also emphasized that livestock covered under the Mass Vaccination Program are protected from disease outbreaks, safeguarding access to local and export markets.

Our focus remains on protecting livelihoods and strengthening resilience.

I was hosted by Turkana County Deputy Governor Hon. Dr John Erus, Loima Constituency MP Hon. Protus Akuja among other leaders.

text:
Bismillah!
Ah! Mash allah! Welcome, welcome, my dear friends. Sit. Observe. Let us talk, , about this… this sweet phenomenon we are witnessing, from Rift valley, Laikipia, Narok to sundrenched N.E Kenya. This new… aesthetic of power.
You see, in the high offices of Nairobi, a new breed of pastoralist has been born. Not from the dust of the plains, but from the air-conditioned boardrooms. They have discovered livestock! A miraculous conversion! One day they are passing Finance Bills, the next, they are pondering the existential mood of a Boran heifer or Somali camel.
These are not your ordinary herders. These are Feedlot Fellows. Instagram pastoralists. They undertake the sacred nomadic journey from the parking lot of a five-star hotel to the plush garden party. Their "migration" is determined by the diary of a PA, not the patterns of the rain. Their "search for greener pastures" is the next fatty tender.

A true nomad, my friend, an Organic Original, has a relationship with the land written in scars and survival. He knows the thirst of the herd in his own throat. His bank is the health of his calves; his insurance is the wisdom of his ancestors. He battles sun, floods and disease, and his joy at a new birth is a profound, silent prayer.

Can the man who flies by chopper to his "ranch" to take a selfie with a bewildered camel, then flies back for a nyama choma fundraiser, understand this? Can he comprehend the weight of a drought? No! His only drought is a delayed government LPO. His "herd" is a collection of luxury assets, grazing on watered lawns, tended by a salaried farm manager he calls "my herdsman."
They pose with sticks they have never used to ward off a real predator! They wear polished beads.  They speak of "our culture" from the terraces of members only clubs!
We, the people of North, are not blind. We see the organic nomad in Turkana,Wajir,Marsabit, Samburu , in the vast and demanding North - enduring, persevering, the true custodians of a resilient spirit. And we see the Artificial Nomads in their bullet-proof cars, playing dress-up with a heritage written in struggle.
Let them keep their hobby cattle and their Instagram camels. But let them not insult our intelligence by draping themselves in a glory they have not earned, in a culture whose hardships they have commodified into a photo-op.

text:
#whyilovekenya 

Pastoralist communities along the northern frontier—from Garissa to Mandera and across Marsabit, Turkana, and Pokot—regularly move across these regions in search of water and pasture for their livestock. 

For these communities, national borders hold little practical significance; survival, particularly during severe droughts such as the one currently unfolding after the failure of the short rains, remains their primary concern. 

My late father, a dedicated veterinarian in the Ministry of Livestock, often spent up to four months away from home as he traversed northern Kenya and occasionally crossing into Ethiopia to vaccinate cattle on both sides of the border in order to prevent disease outbreaks. 

Those of you who think they have found political gum to chew poleni sana , there is none. Not everyone leads a Carefour or Naivas life.  If anything they ought to be commended for making it to a ballot station. 

Tembea Kenya , Kenya ni kubwa sana. 

As always I choose to remain an optimist
